extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, combinatorists, and theoretical computer scientists interested in existence proofs using randomness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for proving existence (or nonexistence) of combinatorial objects by analyzing a suitable random model: compute probabilities or expectations, use tail/union/local-lemma bounds, and possibly postprocess a random sample to obtain a deterministic object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence via positive probability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the probability that a random object chosen from the collection has the property is nonzero, then some object in the collection must possess the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic contrapositive idea of the probabilistic method: showing Pr(property)>0 implies existence. Use an explicitly defined probability space on the class of objects and compute or bound the probability of the desired event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence via expected count < 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the expected number of 'bad' configurations (or of the property you want to avoid); if the expectation is strictly less than 1, then there exists a sample with zero such bad configurations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: compute the expected number of monochromatic r-subgraphs and show E[X] = {n  r} 2^{1-{r  2}} < 1; since the count is a nonnegative integer, some coloring yields 0 bad subgraphs. This technique leverages linearity of expectation and the integrality of counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove nonexistence-of-property by showing probability < 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing the probability is strictly less than 1 can be used to prove the existence of an object that does not satisfy the prescribed properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you want to prove that there exists an object failing a property: demonstrate Pr(all objects have the property) < 1, so some object lacks it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of expectation without independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of expectations is the expectation of the sum regardless of whether the variables are independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows computing expected counts of structures (e.g., number of monochromatic r-subgraphs) by summing the expectations of indicator variables, even when indicators are dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Markov's inequality to bound rare large values
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Markov's inequality to bound the probability that a nonnegative random variable exceeds a given threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bound Pr(X > n/2) for the number of short cycles by applying Markov's inequality to E[X] and showing the probability is o(1) for large n. Useful for controlling counts of undesirable small substructures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Chernoff (concentration) bounds for tail control
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Chernoff bounds to get exponentially small tail bounds for sums of independent indicator variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a common tool: use Chernoff bounds when you have sums of independent random variables (e.g., degrees, counts) and need strong concentration estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Lovász local lemma for limited dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Lovász local lemma to handle collections of bad events that are not independent but have limited dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a standard tool when events are locally dependent and the union bound would be too weak; useful to show positive probability of avoiding all bad events under dependency constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and tune the random model / parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate probability distribution (random model) and tune parameters (e.g., edge probability p in G(n,p)) so that the desired properties hold with positive probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the second Erdős example choose p = n^{1/g - 1} so expected counts of short cycles and independence numbers behave so that required properties occur with high probability. Parameter selection is central to making probabilistic estimates work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine separate positive-probability events to get joint occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Show different desirable properties each hold with sufficiently large probability (e.g., > 1/2 or tending to 1) so that their conjunction has positive probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the random-graph example, show Property 1 holds with prob > 1/2 and Property 2 holds with prob > 1/2; since their probabilities cannot be disjoint, there exists a graph with both properties. Use union bound/complement arguments as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postprocess random sample to obtain exact deterministic object
rubrics_metrics.description: After sampling a random object that likely has approximate desired properties, apply deterministic modifications (e.g., remove vertices or edges) to obtain a final object satisfying the exact requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: remove at most n/2 vertices from a random graph that has few short cycles to obtain a smaller graph with no short cycles while retaining a large chromatic number. Postprocessing converts probabilistic existence into an explicit constructed object (though not necessarily algorithmically found).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge nonconstructive limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic-method proofs are often nonconstructive: they prove existence but do not provide an explicit example or an efficient algorithm to find one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this weakness when algorithmic or explicit constructions are required; many probabilistic existence results leave open the problem of finding explicit examples or efficient constructive algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace probabilistic arguments by counting when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some probabilistic arguments have direct combinatorial counting alternatives that yield the same existence conclusion without invoking probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote example: instead of probabilistic expectation one can count total colorings and bound the number of bad colorings to show a good coloring exists. Consider counting arguments as an alternative or complementary approach.
